items.question: A national museum's cataloguing service writes model output straight into a collections database with mandatory fields. The prompt asks for JSON and defines every field. Which TWO controls must exist between the model and the database, in addition to the prompt asking for JSON? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A retry that re-issues the request with a different temperature on each attempt until something parses.
options.B: A line in the prompt explaining that malformed JSON will break the cataloguing pipeline downstream.
options.C: Validation of the response against the schema at the service boundary, before the record is written.
options.D: A repair step that quietly fixes trailing commas and unquoted keys and passes the record on unlogged.
options.E: A defined path for responses that fail validation — an explicit error or a dead-letter queue a human works.

items.question: A construction group feeds extracted purchase-order data from site paperwork into cost reporting. Records validate against the schema, yet reconciliation keeps failing: some orders show a delivery date the paperwork never carried, and currency amounts from continental European suppliers occasionally land an order of magnitude out. Which TWO additions to the prompt's output contract address these failures? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A maximum word count of 200 words for any free-text field in the extracted record.
options.B: An explicit statement of what to emit when a value is absent from the source document.
options.C: The name and contact details of the team that owns the downstream cost-reporting system.
options.D: Canonical formats for dates, currency and units, including the decimal and thousands convention.
options.E: A self-assessed confidence score per field, which reporting uses to decide whether to accept the record.

items.question: A template interpolates a customer's open support tickets as a list. The renderer takes them from a query with no ORDER BY, so the same customer's prompt is assembled in a different order on different requests. Which consequence should most concern the prompt owner?

options.A: Identical inputs produce different prompts, so behaviour cannot be attributed and no prefix is reused.
options.B: The rendered prompt exceeds the template's declared token budget more often than before.
options.C: The model refuses to process a ticket list whose ordering the template never specifies.
options.D: Template variables must be listed alphabetically for the renderer to substitute them correctly in order.

items.question: A veterinary telemedicine platform stores prompt text in a versioned registry, while temperature and top-p are set per service in environment configuration. A prompt version that scored well in the offline suite behaves noticeably differently in the triage service, and an investigation finds the suite ran at one temperature and the service at another. Nobody considers either setting wrong; they were configured by different teams a year apart.

options.A: Standardise every service and the offline suite on temperature zero so the variable is eliminated entirely.
options.B: Make the sampling settings part of the versioned prompt artefact, so a version identifies text and settings together.
options.C: Record the temperature used in each eval report so reviewers can account for the difference when reading results.
options.D: Run the suite at four temperatures and publish the resulting range of scores for each prompt version.

items.question: A vehicle-leasing company is building a multi-turn negotiation assistant. Its examples currently sit in the system prompt as a block of transcript text under a heading, and the model frequently produces both sides of the exchange — writing the customer's next line as well as its own. The examples themselves are considered good; the team wants the same demonstrations without the role bleed.

options.A: Prefix each line of the transcript with the speaker's name so the roles are unambiguous within the block.
options.B: Reduce the examples to the assistant's turns only, dropping the customer lines from each transcript.
options.C: Add an instruction that the model must never write the customer's side of the conversation under any circumstances.
options.D: Carry the examples in the message list as alternating user and assistant turns before the live conversation.

items.question: A tax authority runs eleven assistants that all include a shared 'source citation' fragment owned by a central platform team and referenced as 'latest'. Overnight the platform team released a fragment change; this morning three of the eleven services show citation-format failures in production, the other eight look normal, and the platform team reports its own tests passed. The eleven services have separate eval suites of varying quality. What should be done next?

options.A: Pin all eleven services to the previous fragment version, then have each team evaluate the new one before adopting it.
options.B: Ask the platform team to revert the fragment release, since its change is what caused the failures.
options.C: Have the three failing services override the shared fragment with their own local copy of the previous text.
options.D: Add citation-format assertions to the eight passing services' suites before deciding anything, so the true blast radius is known.

items.question: A marketplace extracts product attributes across 3,000 categories. A prototype replaces the fixed eight-example block with five examples retrieved per request from a labelled library of 20,000, and quality on long-tail categories improves clearly. The architect must approve it for production, where support regularly asks the team to explain a specific bad extraction from three weeks ago. Which objection must be answered before approval?

options.A: Dynamic selection removes the need for the eval suite to maintain example coverage of its own, since selection adapts.
options.B: Every request carries a different example block, so a past output cannot be rebuilt unless the selection is logged and the library versioned.
options.C: Retrieved examples cannot be carried in the system prompt, so the assistant's role framing must move into the user turn.
options.D: Nearest-neighbour selection will always return five examples sharing one label, which biases every output toward that label.

items.question: A hotel group's rate-audit step asks for a tag-structured response nested five levels deep. Parsing failures cluster at the two deepest levels, usually a closing tag that never arrives, and a failed response yields nothing usable. Which change addresses the cause?

options.A: Increase max_tokens from 2,048 to 8,192 so the deep structures have room to close.
options.B: Instruct the model to check that every tag it opened has been closed before finishing its response.
options.C: Shorten the tag names to three characters so the structural overhead per level is smaller.
options.D: Flatten the output to shallow named blocks that carry identifiers for the nested relationships.

items.question: A field-sales assistant has a paragraph in its system prompt describing when to look up an account in the CRM. The CRM tool's own description was updated last month to narrow the same guidance, and the paragraph was not. The tool is also used by two other assistants owned by different teams. Support sees the assistant looking up accounts in situations the updated description excludes.

options.A: Keep the when-to-use guidance in the tool definition only and let the system prompt describe the assistant's task.
options.B: State in the system prompt that its CRM paragraph takes precedence over the tool's own description whenever they differ.
options.C: Remove the descriptions from the tool definitions and describe all tool behaviour in each assistant's system prompt.
options.D: Add worked examples of correct and incorrect CRM lookups to the system prompt so that the narrowed boundary is shown.

items.question: An online retailer's returns classifier carries eight few-shot examples, a cap set by the token budget for a high-volume path, so admitting a candidate means removing an incumbent. A curator reviews candidates weekly. Which TWO criteria should decide admission? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The candidate discriminates between two categories that no current example separates.
options.B: The candidate was drawn from the most recent week of production returns traffic.
options.C: The candidate is longer than the incumbents, giving the model more signal to work from.
options.D: The candidate belongs to an error class that the evaluation shows the set consistently getting wrong.
options.E: The candidate's output is the phrasing the team would most like to see reproduced word for word.

items.question: A mortgage servicer runs a quality-assurance step that judges whether a recorded call contained a compliance breach. To remove conversational preamble, an engineer prefills the assistant turn with 'The call is compliant because'. Preamble disappears and the reviewer-agreement metric drops sharply. What is the defect?

options.A: The prefilled tokens add to the input length and so to the latency of every call.
options.B: A prefill must be a complete sentence, or the continuation from it reads as ungrammatical.
options.C: The prefill states the verdict, leaving the model to justify a conclusion it has not reached.
options.D: Prefilled text is discarded before generation begins, so the prefill has no effect on the response.

items.question: In a customer-facing prompt, 'do not be too technical' is generally weaker than 'define any term a first-year apprentice would not know' mainly because the second:

options.A: Is the shorter of the two and therefore consumes fewer tokens per request.
options.B: States a target the model and a reviewer can both apply to a specific sentence.
options.C: Is phrased more courteously, which tends to improve the model's compliance.
options.D: Avoids negation, which the Messages API does not reliably support in system prompts.

items.question: A mental-health support service maintains one system prompt containing, among other things, a crisis-escalation section written with a clinical safety lead. Engineers make roughly twenty prompt changes a month, nearly all of them wording and formatting. The service needs the escalation behaviour protected without making every routine change wait on clinical review. Which TWO controls achieve that? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Require the clinical safety lead to review every one of the twenty monthly prompt changes so nothing is missed.
options.B: Register the escalation section as owned by the clinical safety lead, so only diffs touching those lines need that review.
options.C: Permit engineers to edit wording in the escalation section provided they attest the meaning is preserved.
options.D: Auto-approve any change that passes the existing eval suite, on the basis that the suite already encodes the service's requirements.
options.E: Maintain a regression case set for escalation behaviour that must pass before any prompt version becomes releasable.

items.question: A car-hire company's assistant applies a cleaning fee when a vehicle is returned soiled. Three exceptions were added over two years, each as a standalone sentence in a different part of the prompt: top-tier loyalty members, severe-weather events, and pre-existing soiling noted at pickup. Outputs are consistent when one exception applies and inconsistent when two apply at once — the case that generates most complaints.

options.A: Move the three exception sentences so they sit immediately after the cleaning-fee rule they modify.
options.B: Instruct the model to apply whichever exception is most favourable to the customer when more than one is relevant.
options.C: Rewrite the rule and exceptions as one ordered decision procedure with a defined outcome when conditions overlap.
options.D: Add one worked example for each of the three exceptions, each showing the cleaning fee waived.

items.question: A classification prompt on a path handling roughly two million requests a day carries a few-shot block. The strongest reason to keep that block small is that:

options.A: Every example is paid for on every request, so each must discriminate a case the set does not cover.
options.B: The model can attend to only a small fixed number of examples within any one request.
options.C: Prompts above a certain token length stop being eligible for prompt caching at all.
options.D: Longer prompts cause the model to produce proportionally longer output for the same task.

items.question: A payroll provider must replace a decimal `gross_pay` field in its model output with an integer minor-units field, after a rounding discrepancy in one currency. Six internal consumers read the output; they release on different trains, and two are quarterly. The prompt owner controls only the prompt and its output contract. Regulatory reporting depends on two of the consumers being correct throughout.

options.A: Swap the field in one release and coordinate a single cutover date on which all six consumers deploy together.
options.B: Keep the decimal field as the contract and have the two consumers that care about rounding convert it themselves.
options.C: Publish both field names as acceptable and let each consumer's parser accept whichever of them it finds.
options.D: Emit both fields for a deprecation window, let consumers migrate on their own trains, and drop the decimal one in a later version.

items.question: A music-streaming support team has a prompt engineer who iterates in a web console and hands finished prompts to engineering. The latest version scores well in the console and behaves noticeably worse in the service. The prompt text in the repository matches what the engineer pasted. The engineer proposes another iteration in the console to close the gap. What should happen first?

options.A: Keep iterating in the console until the service's behaviour matches it, treating the service as the target.
options.B: Raise the service's temperature until it matches the variability observed in the console runs.
options.C: Capture the request the service sends and diff it against the console request, whitespace and settings included.
options.D: Add more few-shot examples to the prompt until the service's outputs stabilise on their own.

items.question: An airline's disruption assistant interpolates a passenger's rebooking history, which for a few frequent flyers runs to hundreds of entries. The renderer enforces a size budget by truncating the assembled prompt from the end. Investigation of a run of odd outputs finds that for those passengers the output contract, which sits last, had been cut off entirely.

options.A: Truncate the assembled prompt from the beginning instead, so the sections that sit at the end are preserved.
options.B: Apply the budget to the history variable alone, dropping whole entries oldest-first and saying so in the prompt.
options.C: Raise the renderer's size budget so that even the longest rebooking histories fit inside it comfortably.
options.D: Summarise the rebooking history with a preliminary model call and interpolate that summary instead of the entries.

items.question: A utility's billing assistant received a new rule about disputed meter readings, appended to the end of a 4,000-token system prompt. It is followed inconsistently. Review finds an older, looser sentence about disputed readings sitting in the middle of the prompt's account-handling section, written before the new policy. Which TWO changes should be made? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Set the new rule in bold capitals so that it stands out clearly from the surrounding text.
options.B: Repeat the new rule in three separate sections of the prompt so the model encounters it more than once.
options.C: Remove the older, looser sentence about disputed readings, which contradicts the new rule.
options.D: Place the rule inside the account-handling section that governs this behaviour rather than at the end.
options.E: Add the rule to every rendered user turn as well as keeping it in the system prompt.

items.question: A heritage funding body drafts grant-decision feedback letters that a programme officer edits and sends. An audit requires that each letter's decision code and the criteria cited be recorded. An engineer proposes decomposing the whole letter into a nine-field schema returned through a tool, arguing that structured output is more auditable. Officers currently rewrite about a fifth of drafts; the letters are read by unsuccessful applicants.

options.A: Adopt the nine-field schema, since structured output is the more auditable choice wherever an audit requirement exists.
options.B: Adopt the nine-field schema and add a second call that renders those fields back into a letter for the officer.
options.C: Keep the letter as free prose and extract the decision code and the criteria afterwards with a separate model call.
options.D: Structure only what the audit needs — the decision code and criteria cited — and keep the letter body as prose.

items.question: A ferry operator's assistant told a passenger, in a publicly shared screenshot an hour ago, that a cancelled sailing was not refundable when the published policy says it is. The behaviour is not new — the current prompt has always been wrong on this case — and the previous version was wrong in the same way. Prompts are held in a registry with runtime version resolution and a regression suite that runs in about eight minutes. What should the team do next?

options.A: Reproduce the case, add it to the regression suite, and ship a narrow prompt change once the suite passes.
options.B: Edit the live prompt directly in the production environment and confirm the fix by re-asking the same question.
options.C: Pin the assistant back to the previous prompt version in the registry while a proper fix is developed.
options.D: Take the assistant offline until a full review of every refund-related behaviour is complete.

items.question: A pharmaceutical company's medical-information assistant must not state an off-label indication for any product. The team's prompt style guide, written after a maintenance review, says to prefer positive instructions over prohibitions. An engineer proposes deleting the off-label prohibition and replacing it with 'discuss approved indications only', citing the style guide. The medical-affairs lead is uneasy but cannot articulate why.

options.A: Apply the style guide as written, since the positive form covers the same ground and the guide exists to be applied consistently.
options.B: Keep both the prohibition and the positive instruction as written, so the boundary is stated twice from two directions.
options.C: Delete the prohibition and rely on a trained output classifier to catch off-label statements before they reach the user.
options.D: Keep the prohibition for this categorical regulated boundary, pair it with what to say when asked, and add a regression case.

items.question: A prompt pull request is described as 'the same prompt, just reformatted for readability' — line breaks changed, sections reordered, a bulleted list turned into prose. Before release, the team should:

options.A: Release without running the suite, since the semantics of the prompt are unchanged.
options.B: Run the full evaluation suite, because layout, ordering and whitespace can all change behaviour.
options.C: Bump only the patch version and skip review, reserving evaluation for changes to instruction text itself.
options.D: Evaluate only if the reformatting changed the rendered prompt's token count materially.

items.question: A housing association's repair-triage assistant has been through six prompt iterations in eight weeks and sits at 88% agreement with the trades supervisor. Error analysis on the remaining 12% finds that nine in ten of those cases have a tenant description of three words or fewer — 'boiler broken', 'leak' — and that the photograph tenants attach at intake is stored but never passed to the model. Product asks the prompt owner for a seventh iteration.

options.A: Report that prompt work cannot move the residual error, and propose passing the photograph and improving capture.
options.B: Add few-shot examples showing how to triage three-word descriptions like 'leak' and 'boiler broken' correctly.
options.C: Add an instruction to reason step by step about the most likely fault before assigning a trade.
options.D: Ask the model to state a confidence level per case and route low-confidence ones to the trades supervisor for review.

items.question: An architect is drawing up a per-request token budget for a Claude agent. Which set of elements all compete for the same context window?

options.A: Only the current user message and any retrieved documents; system prompts and tool schemas sit outside the window and are injected by the platform at inference time.
options.B: Input tokens only; generated output is discarded after each turn and never re-enters the window on subsequent turns of the same conversation.
options.C: The system prompt and conversation history only; tool definitions and their results are held server-side against the session and do not consume request tokens.
options.D: System prompt, tool definitions, every retained turn, retrieved documents and tool results.

items.question: A freight brokerage runs a Claude agent that works one load-booking task through as many as 90 tool calls, hitting carrier APIs and a rate database. Runs now fail near the end because the transcript outgrows the window and the request is rejected. The team is adding compaction. Which trigger design is soundest for production?

options.A: Measure token utilisation before each model call and compact once it crosses a threshold that leaves headroom for the largest expected tool result and the reply.
options.B: Compact every 20 tool calls, since telemetry shows past runs crossed the limit somewhere around that point in the trajectory.
options.C: Compact only after a request is rejected for exceeding the window, then summarise and replay the failed step — the error is the cheapest possible signal to act on.
options.D: Instruct the model in the system prompt to summarise its own history whenever it judges the transcript to be getting long, and let it self-manage the budget.

items.question: A telco's support assistant sends, on every turn, a large system block of policy and tone rules, a per-customer profile, and the live conversation. The profile is currently prepended above the policy text. Repeat-turn cost is far higher than the team modelled, and almost no request reuses a cached prefix. Which change addresses the cause?

options.A: Shorten the policy text so fewer tokens are re-sent on each turn, and leave the profile where it is.
options.B: Move the entire system block into the first user message so the whole conversation becomes one contiguous cacheable region.
options.C: Keep a separate cached prefix per customer by keying it on customer id, so each customer's profile is cached together with the policy text.
options.D: Keep the invariant policy text as the leading prefix and move the per-customer profile below it, into turn content.

items.question: An insurer's claims adjudication assistant reads a policy wording bundle plus the claim file — often well over a hundred thousand tokens — and applies a 40-rule checklist held in the system prompt. Compliance sampling shows the first eight and last six rules are applied reliably; rules in the middle are skipped, and the skip rate rises with bundle size. The same checklist on short synthetic bundles shows no gap. What is the most likely cause and the right first fix?

options.A: The middle rules are ambiguously worded; rewrite them with worked examples so the model can apply them consistently.
options.B: The request exceeds the context window and the middle of the prompt is being silently truncated; chunk the bundle and process the parts in sequence.
options.C: Recall of mid-prompt material degrades as total length grows; restate the checklist adjacent to the task instruction and apply it in explicit passes over the bundle.
options.D: The capability tier is under-specified for a task of this complexity; move to a higher tier, which will hold the full rule set reliably regardless of bundle length or structure.

items.question: Which condition most favours loading a corpus directly into the context window instead of putting it behind a retrieval step?

options.A: The corpus is small and stable, and answering requires reasoning that spans most of the documents at once.
options.B: The corpus is large and refreshed hourly, and users ask narrow single-fact lookup questions.
options.C: Cost per request is the dominant constraint and the corpus grows every month.
options.D: Answers must quote an exact source passage, and the corpus contains many near-duplicate documents of uncertain provenance.

items.question: A utility runs a Claude agent that migrates 400 legacy report definitions one at a time across a multi-hour session. Engineers need the run to survive both compaction and a mid-run process restart. Which TWO practices make an external scratchpad genuinely load-bearing here? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Keep the scratchpad as an assistant message the agent rewrites each turn, so its current state is always visible without spending a tool call to read it.
options.B: Have the agent write each completed migration's outcome and the next pending item to a durable file immediately on finishing it, and re-read that file after any compaction.
options.C: Copy the full scratchpad into every compaction summary so its entire contents stay resident in the window at all times.
options.D: Give the scratchpad a fixed schema so a partially written entry is detectable and the agent can resume from a known point deterministically.
options.E: Keep the remaining-items list in the agent's reasoning and re-derive progress by re-querying the target system at the start of each turn.

items.question: A fintech's code-review agent begins each run by loading all 90 files a service touches, then answers the reviewer's question. On large services it exceeds the window, and reviewers also report it misses details in files it demonstrably did load. The team already ships a working file-search tool and a file-read tool. What should they do next?

options.A: Pre-generate a summary of each of the 90 files and load the summaries instead, keeping the same load-everything-up-front shape but at a fraction of the tokens.
options.B: Load a repository map of paths, sizes and one-line purposes, then let the agent search and read individual files on demand as the question requires.
options.C: Fan the 90 files across nine parallel sub-agents and have an orchestrator merge their findings into a single review.
options.D: Raise the retrieval top-k so the most relevant files rank higher in the initial load and marginal ones fall away.

items.question: Beyond parallelism, what does giving a sub-agent its own context window do for the parent agent?

options.A: Sub-agent tokens are not counted against the account's usage, so exploratory work effectively becomes free to the parent.
options.B: The parent can share its cached prefix with the sub-agent, so the sub-agent's calls reprocess only their new content.
options.C: The sub-agent's intermediate exploration never enters the parent's window; only its distilled result does.
options.D: Sub-agent results are deterministic, so the parent can cache them by task description and skip repeated work.

items.question: A hospital group's patient-messaging assistant runs behind a stateless HTTP service deployed across three regions with round-robin routing. Threads can stay open for days. The team currently holds transcripts in each pod's memory and loses conversations whenever a pod recycles. Which design fixes this with the least new failure surface?

options.A: Turn on sticky sessions at the load balancer so every request in a conversation is routed back to the pod that already holds it in memory.
options.B: Persist the canonical message list in a shared store keyed by conversation id, and rebuild the prompt from it on every request.
options.C: Have the assistant restate the running conversation inside each reply, so the next turn can be reconstructed from the last message alone.
options.D: Move the transcript to the client and send the whole thing with each request, keeping it in the browser's local storage between visits.

items.question: A retail marketplace's seller-support agent reaches its context ceiling on long escalation threads and must prune. The agent still has to resolve the open dispute and produce an answer a compliance reviewer can reconstruct. Which THREE are the safest to remove first? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Raw payloads of tool results whose conclusions have already been written into the running summary.
options.B: The escalation policy in the system prompt, on the grounds that the agent has already applied it once in this thread.
options.C: Superseded drafts of the reply that the seller explicitly rejected, keeping only the stated reason for rejection.
options.D: The order id and refund amount the seller supplied, since the audit log outside the window already records both values.
options.E: Greeting and pleasantry turns on both sides that carry no decision content.

items.question: When an agent's transcript is compacted part-way through a task, which content has the strongest claim to verbatim carry-over rather than paraphrase?

options.A: The earliest turns in the conversation, because they establish what the task originally was.
options.B: The complete text of every tool result received so far, so that no observation is lost.
options.C: The model's reasoning traces, so the summary can explain how the agent reached its current position.
options.D: Identifiers, exact values, and decisions still open and awaiting action.

items.question: A grid operator's incident agent calls a telemetry API that can return tens of thousands of sensor rows per call. Placing them in the transcript saturates the window within about three calls. The agent's job is to identify anomalous sensors and the time windows in which they misbehaved. What should the integration return to the model?

options.A: The first several hundred rows with an explicit truncation marker, so the agent knows the result is partial and can request the remainder if needed.
options.B: Every row, serialised as CSV rather than JSON — the same information at a materially lower token count per row.
options.C: Per-sensor aggregates and flagged excursions, plus a handle for fetching raw rows for one named sensor.
options.D: Every row, with a standing instruction that the agent must summarise the result into a scratchpad file before it takes any further action.

items.question: In a single call that contains one long document and a question about it, where does the question generally belong relative to the document?

options.A: Before the document, so the model knows what it is looking for while it reads.
options.B: Split across the document, with framing before and the specific ask afterwards.
options.C: After the document, near the end of the prompt.
options.D: Interleaved after each section of the document, so each part is queried locally as it is read.

items.question: A streaming service's content-metadata assistant handles long analyst sessions. To control spend, an engineer added a pruner that drops the oldest user/assistant pair once the transcript passes a size threshold. After the change, cost per session rose rather than fell, and median latency increased. What explains this?

options.A: A shorter transcript forces the model to work harder to reconstruct what was dropped, which inflates output tokens and drives both cost and latency upward.
options.B: Dropping the oldest turns mutates the prompt prefix, so the previously reusable leading region no longer matches and each turn reprocesses from the beginning.
options.C: The pruner issues its own model call every turn to decide what to drop, and that extra round trip accounts for the added latency and cost.
options.D: With less history available the assistant asks more clarifying questions, adding turns to each session and multiplying the per-turn fixed cost.

items.question: An architect is deciding how many retrieved passages to place in the window per request. What is the principal risk of setting that count generously high?

options.A: The retriever begins returning duplicate passages, which the API rejects as malformed content blocks.
options.B: Recall falls, because a reranker only scores the top few candidates it is handed.
options.C: Latency is unaffected, but output tokens rise in proportion to the number of passages supplied.
options.D: Marginally relevant passages dilute the signal and can pull the answer toward the wrong source.

items.question: A logistics platform's agent carries 60 tool definitions, each with a long description and a deeply nested schema. The definitions alone consume a large share of every request, and tool-selection accuracy has degraded as tools were added. Which TWO changes address both problems at once? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Move the tool definitions out of the tools parameter and describe them as prose in the system prompt, where they can be written far more compactly.
options.B: Route each request to a narrowed tool set chosen by task class, exposing only the tools that class can legitimately use.
options.C: Add more few-shot examples demonstrating correct tool choice, covering all 60 tools so the model has a worked case for each.
options.D: Lower max_tokens so the model commits to a tool call sooner instead of deliberating across the full catalogue.
options.E: Collapse families of near-identical tools into a single tool with a discriminating parameter.

items.question: A car maker must extract 30 warranty-relevant clauses from each supplier contract. Contracts run 150 to 400 pages and the longest exceed the window. Twenty-eight of the clauses depend only on their own section; two require reconciling defined terms used throughout the document. The job runs nightly in batch with no latency pressure. What is the right processing shape?

options.A: Send each contract in one call, truncating the longest from the tail where boilerplate normally sits.
options.B: Index every contract in a vector store and retrieve top passages per clause, keeping each call small and uniform in size.
options.C: Process sections strictly in sequence, carrying the accumulated extraction forward so that each later section is judged against everything already found earlier in the same contract.
options.D: Section the contract, extract in parallel per section, then run a focused second pass over the definitions sections and the candidate spans for the two cross-cutting clauses.

items.question: A benefits agency's caseworker assistant compacts at a fixed utilisation threshold. After each compaction the agent re-runs eligibility checks it had already completed, and it has occasionally contradicted a determination it made earlier in the same case. Which TWO items belong in the compaction output to stop this? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The full text of every policy document the agent read before compaction, so that no supporting evidence is lost from the case.
options.B: The agent's step-by-step reasoning for each determination, reproduced verbatim so the chain of logic remains inspectable.
options.C: The determinations already made, each with its rule identifier and a reference to the evidence it rested on.
options.D: The open questions and the next planned action, so the agent resumes the case rather than restarting it.
options.E: A stated remaining token budget for the rest of the run, so the agent can pace its remaining work.

items.question: In context engineering, the term "context rot" refers to which observed behaviour?

options.A: Performance on a task degrades as total context length grows, even when the needed information is present.
options.B: A cached prompt prefix reaches the end of its lifetime and has to be reprocessed from scratch on the next request.
options.C: A summary drifts progressively further from the source as it is re-summarised across successive compactions.
options.D: Retrieved passages become stale relative to the source system because the index refresh lags behind the underlying corpus.

items.question: A pharmaceutical company's competitive-intelligence agent spawns six sub-agents, one per competitor, each searching news, regulatory filings and trial registries. Each sub-agent currently returns its full working transcript to the orchestrator, which then writes the brief. The orchestrator's window now fills before it can write, and the briefs have become unfocused. What should each sub-agent return instead?

options.A: Its transcript with tool results stripped out, keeping only the sub-agent's own messages, intermediate reasoning and final conclusions.
options.B: A structured finding set — claims, each with a source reference and a confidence — against a schema the orchestrator defined up front.
options.C: A free-text narrative summary of what it found, written in whatever form the sub-agent judges most useful for the brief.
options.D: A pointer to its full transcript in object storage, which the orchestrator reads only when it needs supporting detail.

items.question: A bank's reconciliation agent works a single break for up to two hours, compacting three or four times along the way. A post-incident review finds a run where the agent misread a currency code twelve minutes in, the misreading entered the first compaction summary as an established fact, and every later summary faithfully repeated it. The agent never went back to the source record. Which change most directly addresses this failure mode?

options.A: Record each derived conclusion in the summary with a reference back to the source observation, and require re-verification before any irreversible action.
options.B: Compact less frequently, so fewer summaries are chained together and the original observation stays in the window for longer.
options.C: Use the higher-capability tier for the compaction step, on the basis that a stronger summariser is less likely to propagate an error it has been handed.
options.D: Add a standing system-prompt instruction telling the agent to double-check every fact it relies on before acting.

items.question: An e-commerce team's deployment agent reads the same large infrastructure manifest on most turns of a long session, because different steps need different parts of it. The manifest is big enough that even one resident copy leaves little working room, and the agent typically uses two or three blocks at a time. It does not change during a session. Sessions now hit the ceiling within the hour. What should the team do next?

options.A: Replace the whole-file read with a query tool that returns only the block the agent names.
options.B: Read the manifest once at session start and pin that single copy in the stable leading region of the prompt.
options.C: Add a rule permitting the agent at most three manifest reads per session, forcing it to plan its reads.
options.D: Have the agent summarise the manifest after the first read and work from the summary for the rest of the session.

items.question: A just-in-time context strategy replaces bulk preloading with on-demand fetching by identifier. What does it primarily trade away?

options.A: Answer fidelity, because anything fetched on demand has to be delivered in a compressed form to fit the remaining budget.
options.B: Auditability, since nothing in the design records which items the agent chose to pull into its context.
options.C: Wall-clock latency, because the agent spends extra round trips fetching what it decides it needs.
options.D: The ability to plan, because the agent cannot form a strategy until the whole corpus is resident in the window.

items.question: A government tax-filing assistant re-sends, on every turn, the taxpayer's full prior-year return plus the entire conversation. Past about turn twenty responses are slow and the assistant has begun conflating figures between years. Which TWO changes reduce the window pressure without losing its ability to answer detailed questions about the return? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Replace the full return with an extracted figures table, and expose a tool that fetches any named schedule in full on request.
options.B: Move the full return into the system prompt so it stops counting as conversation history.
options.C: Summarise turns older than the most recent few into a rolling digest, keeping the recent turns verbatim.
options.D: Drop the conversation history each turn and answer from the return alone, since the return is the authoritative source.
options.E: Tag every figure the assistant states with the tax year it came from, and carry the current filing year in the system prompt.

items.question: A SaaS HR platform serves 900 employer tenants. Its policy-question assistant concatenates the tenant's entire handbook — anywhere from twenty to two hundred pages — into the system prompt on every request. Cost now scales with tenant handbook size rather than with usage, large tenants get measurably worse answers than small ones, and onboarding a tenant requires editing a prompt template. What is the core design error?

options.A: The system prompt has simply grown too long and needs to be edited down to the sections that matter most.
options.B: Tenant-variable data is being treated as system-level configuration; the handbook belongs behind retrieval as request-scoped context.
options.C: Tenants should be sharded across separate deployments so each instance carries only the handbooks it serves.
options.D: Handbooks should be pre-summarised once during tenant onboarding, with the resulting summary used in the system prompt from then on.

items.question: A legal research assistant retrieves eight passages per turn and appends them to the transcript. Across a ten-turn session the same three landmark authorities come back repeatedly, and by the end they occupy a large share of the window. The assistant must be able to cite, in its closing memo, any passage it relied on at any point in the session. What is the right handling?

options.A: Reduce top-k from eight to three so that fewer duplicate passages accumulate over the session.
options.B: Clear all retrieved passages at the start of every turn and re-retrieve from scratch for whichever question is currently being asked.
options.C: Keep a per-session set of already-supplied passage identifiers and, on a repeat hit, insert a short reference instead of the passage text.
options.D: Rerank so that passages already shown in this session are demoted below ones the assistant has not yet seen.

items.question: In context management, what distinguishes pruning from compaction?

options.A: Pruning decisions are made by the model during its turn, whereas compaction is performed by the orchestration layer between turns.
options.B: Pruning removes selected content outright; compaction replaces a span of content with a shorter representation of it.
options.C: Pruning applies to retrieved documents in the window, whereas compaction applies to conversation turns.
options.D: Pruning is lossless because it only removes exact duplicates, whereas compaction is inherently lossy.

items.question: An engineering consultancy is designing a standards-lookup assistant over roughly 12,000 technical standards documents, refreshed weekly. Most questions are answered by a single clause; about one in six requires comparing requirements across two or three standards. Which THREE statements should shape the design? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Because some questions span documents, every request should load the full text of all standards the user has asked about earlier in the session.
options.B: The corpus size and weekly refresh make per-request loading of everything impractical, so retrieval has to be the entry point.
options.C: Retrieving clauses first and then loading the full text of the two or three standards those clauses came from handles the comparison cases without inflating the common case.
options.D: Clause-level retrieval alone is sufficient for the comparison cases, because reranking will surface the relevant clauses from each standard together.
options.E: Routing on question type lets the comparative path spend a larger context budget than the single-clause path.

items.question: An insurer's motor-claim triage assistant receives between eight and thirty damage photographs per claim, alongside the adjuster's notes and the policy schedule. On claims at the upper end, requests are rejected for exceeding the context window. The team is surprised, because the text portion is small. What is the correct explanation and remedy?

options.A: The output ceiling is being hit rather than the input one; raise the reply cap so the request has room to complete.
options.B: Images must be converted to structured text descriptions in a preceding call, and only those descriptions passed on to the assessment step.
options.C: Photographs should be sent one per call, with the individual assessments merged into a claim-level view afterwards.
options.D: Images consume context budget in proportion to their dimensions; downscale to the resolution the task needs and select a subset before the call.

items.question: A telco's network-remediation agent runs for up to 200 steps against a single ticket. Operators report that on the longest runs it drifts: by around step 150 it is often improving something adjacent to the ticket rather than closing it. By that point the transcript is dominated by tool output from earlier diagnostics. Which intervention targets the cause?

options.A: Cap runs at 100 steps and escalate anything unresolved at that point to a human engineer.
options.B: Move the objective into the system prompt so that it is stated once, authoritatively and unambiguously, at the very top of every request the agent issues.
options.C: Retain more of the diagnostic tool output, so that the agent has fuller evidence about what the ticket actually involves.
options.D: Regenerate a short structured plan block restating the ticket and the outstanding acceptance criteria, placed immediately before each model turn.

items.question: Which content is best placed in the system prompt rather than in a user turn?

options.A: Durable role, constraints and output rules that apply identically to every request this application makes.
options.B: The specific document the user has asked to have analysed on this particular request.
options.C: The user's most recent instruction, relocated there so that it carries higher priority than earlier ones.
options.D: Retrieved passages, placed there so the model treats them as authoritative rather than as user-supplied claims.

items.question: A logistics firm's agent compacts three to five times during runs that make hundreds of tool calls. The team is deciding which model tier should perform the compaction step. Post-incident reviews show that poor summaries have repeatedly caused the agent to redo work it had already completed. What is the soundest choice?

options.A: Always use the cheapest available tier, since summarising text the model can already see is a straightforward and low-risk task.
options.B: Use the same tier as the agent's own steps, or a stronger one, because compaction is a low-frequency, high-leverage call.
options.C: Use the cheapest tier but run compaction twice and keep the longer of the two summaries.
options.D: Drop the model from the loop entirely and compact by deterministic truncation of the oldest turns.

items.question: A bank's telephone banking assistant works to a hard 900ms budget from the end of caller speech to the start of the spoken reply. Calls average nine turns but can reach forty. Time to first token climbs steadily through a call and breaches the budget past roughly turn 25, because the whole transcript is re-sent each time. Replies must still reflect anything the caller said earlier in the call. What should the team do next?

options.A: Drop everything before the last three turns, which bounds the transcript at a size that comfortably fits the budget.
options.B: Maintain a rolling structured state block — caller intent, accounts referenced, actions taken, outstanding confirmations — updated between turns and sent in place of the older turns.
options.C: Move the entire call onto a faster capability tier from the first turn onward, accepting a measurable loss of answer quality in exchange for the latency headroom the budget demands.
options.D: Enable response streaming so the caller begins hearing the reply while the rest is still being generated.

items.question: A public health agency's outbreak-investigation agent keeps running notes across a multi-day investigation. The team is moving from a freeform note file to one with a fixed schema. Which TWO are genuine reasons to make that change? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Named fields can be loaded selectively, so a given step pulls only the sections it needs rather than the whole note file.
options.B: Structured notes are tokenised more efficiently than prose carrying the same information.
options.C: A schema prevents the model from writing an incorrect value into a field.
options.D: Schema'd notes remove the need to re-read the notes after a compaction, because the structure survives summarisation.
options.E: A required field left unfilled becomes a detectable condition rather than a silent gap in the investigation.

items.question: Why would a production system count the tokens in an assembled prompt before dispatching it, rather than letting the API reject anything oversized?

options.A: Because the token count of a request determines which capability tiers the account is permitted to use for it.
options.B: Because the provider's count and the caller's own count diverge, and the two have to be reconciled for internal chargeback reporting.
options.C: So the request can be reshaped or rerouted — context trimmed, work split, a different path chosen — before the user sees a failure.
options.D: Because a locally computed count is the only way to verify that the prompt template rendered all its variables correctly.

items.question: A manufacturer's quality-investigation agent runs for hours, and its host process is occasionally killed mid-run. Today a restart begins the investigation from scratch. The team wants restarts to resume instead. Which TWO properties must the design have? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The full transcript must be persisted verbatim, so the resumed run can be handed an identical context to the one it lost.
options.B: Each state-changing step must be recorded durably outside the transcript before the following step begins.
options.C: The model must be pinned to a fixed sampling seed so the resumed run reproduces the original trajectory.
options.D: The resume path must rebuild a working context from the durable record rather than attempting to restore the lost transcript.
options.E: Compaction must be disabled during long runs so that no state is lost before the next checkpoint is written.
